title: I See You
review:
I See You

"I dreamed I could bring peace but sooner or later you have to wake up." This is the famous quote by Jake Sully in James Cameron's 2010 hit film, Avatar. The setting is futuristic with dates in 2054 showing the new life in different unknown lands. This film gives a nice contrast between; practical, aesthetic and ethical criteria. The film is a must see and should be viewed by anyone who enjoys a romance, action or even a little comedy.

The relationship between the Avatars and the NáVi people give the practical criteria an interesting flare. When the Avatars go to Pandora, the home of the indigenous beings, they try to build a relationship with them by showing them new skills, teaching them English and showing them American customs. Cameron gives the film a twist of romance through the relationship between Jake and Neytiri, the NáVi leader's daughter.

Romance keeps the story linked between the Avatars world and the "real world". Jake's Avatar builds a strong relationship to his new mate in the NáVi land and becomes a part of their people. Throughout their relationship, Neytiri tells Jake's Avatar that she "sees him", not in a literal sense but in a deep, emotional connection between their souls that their love is growing and drawing them closer together. Not only is romance shown in the movie but the major genre is action. The battle between the two worlds is shown in an intense way and is appealing to young adults; both male and female.

James Cameron did an amazing job in the graphics shown in the film during scenes in the land of Pandora. The aesthetic criteria are fulfilled amazingly throughout the whole film. The colors of the film are unique and extremely eye catching. The film can be seen in 3D which shows an even better visual impact but is still fantastic without that effect. The colors in the land of Pandora are based off of "cool color tones". Plants, NáVi, the Avatars, animals and even specks of dust have exquisite color effects and keep the film viewer's attention throughout the entire film. A flip from the "real world" and the NáVi life is exchanged several times during the film and the scenery is tremendously different. In the "real world", of the American troops and the scientist's station on the land, the colors are dull with no sense of excitement. Whereas when the switch is made to the land of Pandora the whole view of the film is complete opposite, to lively colors of creatures, land and NáVi people. The ethical statement in the film shows that wealth is very controlling. Pandora is a magical land where culture and tradition are key essentials to life. The main reason the military troops are there is to destroy the land of Pandora and obtain a large amount of Unobtainium. Grace and her scientist show a new meaning to the behavior shown to the NáVi people. She, along with the other Avatars, show the people respect to their land and gain their trust. Their morals are shown through their behavior, just like the troops reflect their morals through their behavior. The military colonel shows no respect when speaking of the natives or their land. When Jake's Avatar makes a connection with the sacred Eywa tree and becomes the mate to Neytiri, making him a member of the NáVi people, the NáVi's have a great sense of trust in him. This in return makes the colonel very upset and reflects him as an unethical being. He goes to the land of the NáVi's and tries to kill not only Jake's Avatar but Jake himself. In the sense of negative ethics shown in the film the military troops are only on the land of Pandora for the quest of Unobtainium, a rock in Pandora sold for 20 million dollars a kilogram in the States. Although they are there for this rare rock, there are a few scientists there to help the NáVi people to move from their land safely. Grace, who is in charge of the Avatars, wants to move the NáVi's without violence, yet the nature of the Americans is to start war and move them with bombs and guns.

The ending is amazing and cannot even begin to be explained. Viewers of this film will not be disappointed. Some people would say this is just another love story with no "real world" relevance, but I believe the director did a great job of showing the ethical standpoint while making the graphics extraordinarily astonishing.

I definitely enjoyed every scene of this film and could watch it several times and still become mesmerized by the graphics, the practical storyline and the ethical criteria displayed throughout the entire film. I would recommend this to any viewer who enjoys a nice mixture of action, romance and a bit of comedy. So, what are you waiting for?

title: Tears in the rain
review: There is a fundamental error in Avatar, which director James Cameron refused to see when making the movie. The world of Pandora is brilliant and original indeed, but in no way does it justify alone an almost three hour movie. True art in cinema is rare and it combines a multitude of components such as storyline, character development, mise en scene, music score etc. Cameron focuses 100% in the technical part of the film-which is undoubtedly excellent and innovative-and deliberately neglects everything else. If one accepts that Avatar is a sci-fi adventure with no brains whatsoever, then he will have a great time watching it, but if one enters the world of Pandora with expectations of anything more than that, then he will be very disappointed. No problem here, except we are talking about Cameron, director of The Abyss and Titanic. Those movies had the technical brilliance of their age, but in the same time had everything else. Who can forget Mary Elisabeth Mastrantonio calling for Ed Harris on the walkie as he descents in the dark depths of the ocean or Kate Winslet whispering in the cold and endless waters as she gazes Leonardo Di Caprio vanishing in the dark beneath her, while, just feet away, the titanic makes its final voyage to oblivion. Even when Arnold Schwarzeneger gives his mechanical life to save Eduard Furlog and Linda Hamilton. All these are moments that defined a filmic genre and an age of cinema. Unfortunately, in ten years time, we will still remember these moments, while all of Avatar will be lost...like tears in the rain...

title: Avatar from my POV
review:
Movie critics and Civil Rights activists have always viewed movies with a different perspective than most people. They always look for "racist" hints in movies that are just meant for sheer entertainment. Reading the critiques on movies like Avatar can make one believe that the critic writing the review is racist themselves. They always target white people and make the Caucasian race seem either like bad guys or like unworthy heroes because they're white. Such an example is shown in the reviews for Avatar, the astounding movie that could cause even the most unimaginative person to think of the possibility of life on other planets. The Na'vi people in the movie are tall, blue, catlike humanoids that are very in touch with their deity and the nature of their world. They are spiritual and have some traits of humans, such as their clans and their own language.

Some critics say that they might be imitating African Americans, with the accents and the darker skin tones. Some say they might be imitating native Americans, with references to Pocahontas. I say it's just an amazing and suspenseful movie that will make any person dream of intelligent life on other enchantingly beautiful planets such as Pandora. The accusations of the "racist" and "degrading" aspects of this movie are ludicrous, to say the least. It's meant to appeal to human's imaginative and creative nature and that's it. People just can't seem to enjoy such a work of art without judging it.

If the makers of Avatar were trying to convey any kind of message to us, it would be to love our Mother Earth and end the greed that consumes us. It's getting us nowhere, and just as Jake Sully says in the movie, "If people are sitting on s*** that you want, you make them your enemy." That would be the only message they would be trying to get across IF they were trying to get a message across. It's the only one that makes true sense if you watch the movie with an open mind. It's not being racist at all.

I would recommend Avatar to any action, sci-fi, or romance loving kind of person. It's packed with thrills around every turn. It's so plainly enjoyable and the graphics spell-bindingly realistic that a person will question reality after viewing it. To sum Avatar up in two words, it's an outstanding movie.

title: Beautiful images but lame story
review:
Man I don't know where to start the story of Avatar is a long and predictable one. With all its hype of: 3D, imax, and ground breaking C.G.I. there really wasn't anything left for a decent story to be told. I'll be frank. The movie is beautiful to look at (By beautiful I mean the most: realistic, gorgeous, and imaginative visuals I have ever seen!)but is hampered by a very lame and predictable story. By the time your half way through you'll know what the movie will lead toward and probably guess the ending. So what is so bad about this story? Well I should say it isn't bad but one that we all heard somewhere before not to spoil anything but in a nutshell its somewhat like Disneys Pocahontas and Dances with wolves. Just in the future with blue aliens and not as good. Now I know the budget for this movie was a ridiculous amount what with all that groundbreaking CG; I guess one could debate they wanted to be safe and kept the story and script to formula but they could have done a better job I mean Titanic had that a story we all heard but pulled us in with its characters.

This is where Avatar really fails for me as great movie the characters in the story really aren't that interesting or engaging. I didn't find myself caring about what happens to a lot of them. Some dialogue and sequences from the characters come off as more than a little cliché and at times awkward to sit through. My mind started wandering at certain parts because I wasn't immersed with the characters, or because I knew what might happen and was waiting for it to draw out. I don't know what went wrong when James Cameron the guy who wrote and directed Titanic and the first two Terminators but some re-writing in the script would of helped.

Now I probably bashed this movie so much you think I hate it. Not so. As an experience it really is worth checking out for the sheer spectacle of it all. The visuals really are breathtaking to see and being the first movie in 3D (from what I know) that's good I recommend you go to the nearest imax theater to watch if it still is playing, or rent it. As a movie on its own though it really isn't worth collecting unless you want it for being so groundbreaking. The predictable story and bad character writing at times really do bring down what could of been a classic for me anyway. Especially considering its over two and half hours that is a long time to wait and watch something you know is going to happen.

title: While lots of plot is "recycled" it is a a MUST SEE (Once)
review:
Words can't do justice to the shear quality of the visuals in this movie - 3D or no 3D. On a well calibrated large screen HDTV in 1080p literally every frame is jaw dropping in both quality and imagination, every second the audio is truly immersive and razor sharp.

If you want to show off you shiny Home Theater to friends and family then I can't think of many other movies that are in contention.

Sure, there are large amounts of schlock in the plot, but check your cynicism at the door and enjoy one of the most perfectly blended pieces of CGI & live action created.

The advances in technology that have moved "state of the art" CGI from those in Jurassic Park to Peter Jackson's LoTR Trilogy and now Avatar I'm looking forwards to what's coming next.

Jurassic Park showed that CGI can be convincing (But looks dated these days), Jackson and WETA Digital showed that CGI can be used on a MASSIVE scale and deliver convincing results, and Cameron has proved that you can easily become so immersed in the visuals that you forget that you haven't seen anything "Real" for many scenes.

Mr Lucas needs to take notes because there's literally no contest between his "ground breaking" CGI work on the remastered Star Wars Tilogy (and the best ignored prequels) and Cameron's "State of the art" Avatar.

Now if only the plot and characterizations were better, and "Unobtanium" left as an unnamed element it would warrant a rare 10/10; despite being at it's heart a mediocre rehash.

title: Eh....
review:
Let me caveat this (short) review with the fact that I *didn't* see Avatar on the big screen, and definitely not in 3D. The visuals are spectacular even on TV - and I'm sure they would have been positively mind blowing in IMAX.

Yes, the visuals are beautiful - and the creatures of Pandora well realized (a little too similar to Earth creatures, but still very well rendered.)

But as for the story and acting? Mundane, average, and seen it before. (Which is a shame - I'm a huge fan of both Titanic and Aliens, which I consider one of the top horror/action films ever made...both of which are proof that Cameron can put both amazing visuals *and* story into a film with amazing success.)

But in Avatar's case, the story was basically Ferngully, and had all the obvious, old and overdone stereotypes - from the evil big business profit mongers and the unfeeling military to the eco-conscious and pure native species. Oh, and a 'love story' that was obviously in the works from practically the first scene. No characterization depth at all.

It's a shame. Cameron can do amazing things. But Avatar isn't one of them. Except visually.

title: Visual effects make up for weak story
review:
I suppose the big selling point behind this movie was the special effects, and this film doesn't shy away from getting in your face with some of the most beautiful and amazing images I have ever seen.

The amount of detail and love that went into the visuals is just outstanding. The scenery, the creatures, the Navi, wow!! If you see this movie, see it for the visuals.

Now if only Cameron had put the same amount of care into the script

The plot for this movie seemed to borrow from a number of sources, the two standouts being Dances with Wolves and Pocahontas. I must defend Cameron, as it extremely hard to be 100% original these days, as most ideas have been used time and time before.

Nevertheless, the plot weakened the overall viewing experience. I had a feeling I knew how the movie was going to end. And the movie went for a bit too long; unnecessary points in the plot could have saved the studios a LOT of money.

But in the end, the goods outdo the bads. Avatar's visuals are a good enough reason to see this film, even if the film is more of a "look what we can do" piece rather than a piece of storytelling.

title: Nothing special, beside the Visual effects
review:
There's nothing new, and original, about this Pocahontas look a like, sci- fi movie. Of course beside, the Visual effects, the Sound, and the Art/set direction. That is worth the experience, and money well spent. Because, the whole experience, of the movie, is great it self. But there's nothing new about this movie, if you have seen a action/sci-fi or two, you would know, what will happened, and who will win. (Good VS. Evil).

It's story, is simple, it's almost like Pocahontas, beside Pocahontas dose not take place, in a planet called Pandora.

Worth watching, because of it's great visual effects, but will be forgotten, when a newer movie, with better effects, will take over.

title: Weak plot but not too awful
review:
For a $237 million budget, from a Three-Time-Oscar-Winning director, the first film in years to be shot in 3D, and hype that puts the seventh Harry Potter book to shame, I expected the best film of the decade when I bought tickets for "Avatar". It was far from that...

I don't really need many words to describe the plot. I wont use the Smurf joke as that's been overused, but I can compare this film faultlessly to "Dances With Wolves". An OK plot, but a bit to weak. It's something that would be aimed at the same sort of audience as The Little Mermaid... The very cliché plot was disguised with 3D cinematography. Unfortunately though, if you don't see it in 3D, it exposes what's left of the film. Which is little. Hence why a lot of people I know fell asleep whilst watching it in 2D... though some did fall asleep during the 3D version too. It's real shame, because there were some great ideas, but they weren't developed enough.

However, despite a weak plot, we are provided with some good characters, which is crucial in any film. We get to see plenty of emotions and opinions in this film, which off course leads to an exciting climax. There is an on-going battle almost from the word "go" between the scientists and the military. These are very well developed scenarios, with a clear and believable difference between character relationships. There are no pushovers, and pushovers are very good evidence for a lazy screenwriter. Character wise, everyone is really well developed, and Cameron has kept the realism whilst drafting his characters.

As far as the effects go (which is what propelled this film to the top of the Box Office) some are outstanding, others are dismal. The space craft and explosions are neat, but the CGI and Motion Captured Na'Vi are awful. The tone of them is almost mono... but a film shouldn't rely on great special effects, which unfortunately, this film does.

The acting wasn't that bad either. Considering there was some awful dialogue, the actors executed it well, as did the actresses. Stephen Lang played the bent Colonel Miles Quaritch brilliantly, bringing forward a great impression of a Military Commissioned Officer.

The over hype, weak plot, bad dialogue, and some disappointing CGI doesn't deserve a $3 billion gross, but that's the way the film industry ticks. I don't like to heavily criticise films, as I know the effort that goes into making them. It's definitely worth a watch, but unless you are a huge James Cameron fan, I'd rent this if I were you. (Or record it off the TV)

title: Stunning and imaginative visually, but a stereotypical story full of old clichés
review:
Recap: Mankind has gone for the stars and found a treasure of the rare material Unobtanium in the planet Pandora. Covered by a beautiful but deceptively dangerous jungle a big part of the human colony is security forces, and that is how disabled veteran marine Jake Sully ends up there. Going in place of his dead brother he operates an Avatar to reach out to the humanoid native species, the Na'vi. The Na'vi is in extreme touch with nature, depends and protects it at any cost, and it is soon clear that their interest comes in clear conflict with the humans' greedy mining intentions. And of course, Jake ends up in the middle of this, feeling more and more sympathy for the awe inspiring nature, and finding love with the Na'vi.

Comments: Despite not seeing this in 3D, but only on a Bluray, this still is stunningly beautiful picture with marvelous sceneries, landscapes and vistas, not to mention wonderful details. It is instantly obvious that this is a movie heavy in the visual experience. And despite coming with heavy praise, it doesn't disappoint even though some scenes are clearly solely there to impress 3D-watchers. Still, many scenes are just breathtaking. It is a marvel of light and colour in the hands of a playful, imaginative mind (or more probably, minds). Most impressive, and most entertaining.

But the danger with movies becoming so heavily focused on the visual and effects part is that the story might be somewhat forgotten, or at least having to take the back seat. Avatar, along with 2012 for example, suffers from this. In Avatar's case a very big part of the framework of the story is almost copy-pasted from an old western movie, complete with stereotypes of the evil white ranchers and the primitive but in touch with nature natives. It annoyed me that a movie with such a big budget, and made with such an enormous effort couldn't be more original than that. However, a cliché is often a cliché for a reason, and in this case it is because it provides a simple story with a clear conflict to exploit with stunning effects.

Sam Worthington has quickly established himself as a lead man in action movies. And with good support from Sigourney Weaver, Zoe Saldana, Michelle Roudrigez, Stephen Lang and Joel Moore, among many others, there is absolutely nothing to complain about the cast, or their performances.

In all, Avatar was a refreshingly good movie. Long as it is, something is always happening or there is something breathtaking to watch, it is entertaining every minute, even if predictable. It is a real treat, and I'm thankful that once in a while someone sets their mind's to make an epic film like Avatar (and note that is almost always a sci-fi). Highly recommended, and would have been a full-pointer if there would have been just a little more effort on a more original script.

8/10

title: Visually groundbreaking but story falls short at the end
review: Visually, Avatar is probably the most stylish and groundbreaking film in the history of cinema. Its use of CGIs and visual effects are truly at whole another level from everything else I have seen. This technique may be the first of its kind. This a science fiction/war story with strong dramatic elements. Humans are colonizing another planet due to its rich resources and they engage in a battle with the planet local inhabitants (the blue creatures). At the end, it is a classic battle between strong evil enemy and the less powerful, good guys. I think the ending was contrived and unrealistic. Something about it just didn't feel right. I think it could have been written better, more intelligently, but it felt as if they wanted to bank on the visuals so they stretched the story to include more action scenes which, in my opinion, is the only downfall of this movie. I still think it should have won the best picture (instead of The Hurt Locker).

title: Disney
review: Avatar is a 3D benchmark program married to an early script of Pochahontas. It's a Walt Disney movie and the way it is colorful and fun only underlines the fact how lucrative it is designed to be. The story is about war and extinction, stuff like that is not colorful and fun. Yes, it is a wonder of computer technology, but technological wonders happen every day, just look at your 50 gigs pendrive smaller then your thumbnail, since when do we credit that as art? I do not find avatar a particularly bad movie, but as a general piece of filmmaking it is not worth more praise than a worse Disney vehicle and the way it now forces cinema to convert to a 3D entertainment park is not something I regard as a benefit to the world.

title: Perhaps not for everyone, but I thought it was fantasitic
review: I've just watched the special edition of Avatar and it reminded me of how much I liked this film. Every time I watch it, it leaves me with this feeling which I can't quite explain. Whil I admit, its not perfect and that there are some rough areas and that the plot line is similar to a few other films, I don't feel that these few mistakes ruin the film. The other thing that I like about what David has done is that, while the film is set in the future, you still get a sense of modern day society. You still have the same warning sounds from heavy duty machinery, as well as other features here and there. Overall, I feel that David has made a film that well portrays what would most likely happen if we were to discover a new world and that he has opened new doors in the way that films can be made.

title: Movie Review 1 - UCO 1200
review:
Avatar is a one of a kind film with all of the animation built into it. I enjoyed this movie a lot mainly because I am a graphic design major in college and there was so much work put into Avatar to make bring out the detail in the animation to make it look as realistic as possible. Though this film was almost three hours, I did not find myself restless and ready to leave. The movie kept me tuned in and focused on the plot, which is one of the key factors in developing a successful movie. The plot of Avatar was very good and I towards the end of the movie, I actually wanted the humans to lose. When I think about it, it seems weird because I am human, but James Cameron did a wonderful job with the plot to make my emotions and thoughts turned against my own race. As much as I loved this film there was a few things I did not like about it.

I felt that some of the scenes in Avatar were a little too long. The movie overall was not too long, it just seemed that some of the scenes dragged out longer than they should have. For example, the scene before the sex scene, where they are walking around the secret trees, I think they walk around the talk about the trees for too long. Beside that I cannot think of anything else I disliked about the film. Avatar is also similar to the movie Dances with Wolves.

Dances with Wolves has a similar plot to Avatar's. They are both about a white man who finds a native culture and eventually learns the ways of that culture. The man starts to become part of the natives so much that he is willing to turn against his own kind in order to defend the natives. Avatar is just a more sci-fi type movie, with advanced technology. Avatar was one of the great movies that people will always refer to.

title: Amazing entertainment, not much more
review:
Avatar is the best really big blockbuster since LOTR: The Return of the King, also smashing that movie at the box office. It's an amazing film as long as you don't take it too seriously and consider the quality and originality of the story.

Cameron has tried to make an epic that also delivers a message to the audience. One problem is that the story is so weak and unoriginal. Also the message is so easily discernible, it could just as well be written in plain text at the start of the film... Thus it loses much power.

Avatar works much better for you if you turn your brain off. Then you can let yourself be amazed by the incredible visuals, both people and landscapes look stunningly good and lifelike. I can promise with all my heart that you've never seen anything like it! And please watch it in 3D! This movie is made for 3D, and it really shows how 3D can make a movie into an experience you'll remember for a long time.

title: Saw past the sparkle to nothing underneath
review:
This movie is another shining example of how pretty special effects can hide a story with absolutely no real substance, no imagination, and cliché characters that have been done a million times before. Only reason I didn't give it a 1 was because said visuals were better than most. However, as classic movies exist with absolutely terrible visual effects, we need to fall back on plot, characters, story and message (if it exists, here, it does) into account.

Simply put...if you've seen Fern Gully? You've basically seen this movie already.

All the same elements are in both: a young girl of an indigenous, foresty species...the indigenous boy who likes her...the human that integrates and falls in love with the indigenous young girl...the old indigenous lady who knows everything...and humans razing the beauty of nature in an attempt to make money. This movie's story focuses around Jake, a paralyzed man who takes part in a military operation to another planet (populated by blue Indians...sorry...Native Americans) that involves implanting his consciousness into an artificial version of a member of the indigenous species. The idea is that the government agents in charge hope that he can convince the natives to willfully turn over the source of their energy so that the evil, wicked, despicable humans can steal and rape their land for resources...you know, like humans always do. No chance, by the way, that human special interest groups on Earth would have stopped this before it happened, is there? Nah...

In the process, Jake is able to experience life with his legs again (a really tacked on aspect to add urgency to a character that's so boiler plate, a child could have come up with it). Jake plays the typical white American that goes to another land and attempts to communicate with others by simply speaking English and moving his hands. He quickly meets a girl with a long name that starts with N, that I still can't remember, and whether or not they end up together by the end...well...let's just say, it's pretty predictable.

Not only did James Cameron rip off the idea of humans bringing destruction to a beautiful woodland vicinity in the name of greed, he also made the movie especially topical by ripping off sayings from former President George W. Bush, such as "fight terror with terror," in an attempt to make the humans look even more evil, insensitive and barbaric.

I'm an author that's written numerous books, and I find such tactics in storytelling to be cheap, easy, unimaginative and useless when addressing how high or low creativity standards should lie. It's sad that movie-making greatness is reduced to flashy computer graphics, exploiting references to the most vicious and underhanded attack on American soil in history, and wearing glasses for three hours.

Can't wait for Avatar 2...I hear it's going to take place in the Waters of Pandora...so we're going be underwater, probably more bubble effects...

Lovely...

title: A True Movie Experience!
review: James Cameron scores again! I have seen this terrific film three times now. First in the theater in 3-D, the best way to truly experience its awe and beauty, and twice on Blu-Ray DVD. This film is like nothing you've seen on film before. First off, it is visually stunning and brilliantly imaginative. It has everything a film needs to be a classic: fast paced direction, a fine cast, awesome cinematography by Mauro Fiore, a beautiful music score by the brilliant James Horner, unbelievable special effects by a fabulous crew of hundreds, fantastic sound and sound effects which make one feel like they are there on the planet Pandora. James Cameron is expert at directing wonderful films and he finds such talented people to work with. The cast is overall very good with the likes of Sam Worthington, Zoe Saldana and Sigourney Weaver in the lead roles and such stalwarts as Giovanni Ribisi, Michelle Rodriguez, Wes Studi, CCH Pounder and Stephen Lang in the supporting roles.. Many criticize the storyline, but I find little wrong with it. It borrows from Dances with Wolves, Braveheart and maybe Wall Street. It mainly deals with corporate greed. Topical? Hmmm. It's main selling point is truly the visuals, but the story is involving and the cast is good. I felt Stephen Lang played it a little over-the-top, but that's excusable. Cameron likes a bit of gung hoi-sm in his films. I find that so far the film holds up very well after 3 viewings and I'm sure it will after many more viewings. I wish I had a 3D TV.

title: Avatar isn't really a movie! Its a experience!
review:

*****Warning the rest of this review might contain spoilers*****

Granted the story wasn't ground breaking, its wasn't even new , it had all be done before. But it didn't take me long time watching the movie to realize that avatar is not an ordinary movie, its focus wasn't to tell a story, like other movies, it was to immerse yourself into a beautyfull world, of unimaginable creativity (you can see everything from an lizard helicopters to floating mountains), more like what a video game wants you too then a movie. title: We Came, We Saw, We Conquered, Felt Bad and Made a Movie about it
review:
Some of the conservatives seem to think that Avatar is some kind of "extreme liberal, Anti American propaganda movie". It's not. Avatar is simply too stupid. For an Anti American propaganda movie it's incredibly tame. I could think of 100 different ways to turn this into a real Anti American propaganda movie. But what would be the point? Avatar tries to criticize Western Imperialism, but it's critique is incredibly dull and childish. It's like Disney trying to criticize consumer culture with Donald Duck.

But more than that, Avatar is not a movie. It is a mass consumer event. Spectacle. You don't watch avatar, because there is nothing to watch. There is nothing to think or discover here. Everything is easily accessible and require nothing from the audience. Once again people have to turn their brains off (maybe sometimes the masses should turn their brains on) to consume this mindless spectacle. Movies like Avatar are consumed. For the mass consumers Avatar is a special event to be consumed and then discarded like Michael Jacksons death.

The plot is mindbogglingly boring and clichéd. Everything in this movie is a derivative or lifted from thousand other movies. You have seen this movie before a hundred times. Except in Avatar everything is completely overblown. From the digital forests to the cgi characters, everything is too much. There is no room to breathe, to take in the scenery or to get properly orientated. Then again practically everything is CGI. It's ironic that the supposedly environmentalist movie has only digital forests and digital animals.

The final hour of the movie goes from silly and clichéd to downright insulting. The slap in the face happens when, once again the natives have to be rescued by a white man. Avatar becomes yet another childish fantasy. In movies we always correct our mistakes, side with the natives and exorcise the evil in us. It's completely self defeating and any message Avatar may have had implodes in the end. It's just another silly fantasy, just like the idea that we can save the environment by buying new "environmentally friendly" cars. We need to stop buying and driving cars. We can't consume our way out of this.

And of course Avatar itself took hundreds of millions to make. Lot's of energy has been consumed in producing this movie. Much of that energy comes from coal that adds to environmental problems. Everything in our culture turns into a mass consumer event. Avatar is simply another expression of this. What ever message it has is simply consumed.

In my mind they should have ended the movie with the Na-vi defeat. Na-vis should have been tortured, humiliated and forced to live in small reservations, depraved of their culture and land. The small number of survivors should have then been forced to accept and adapt to the invaders culture. -The End.

But of course Hollywood can't show us the true face of Imperialism, instead they give us silly fantasies.

title: Terrible movie with great effects
review:
What can be said about the movie Avatar that hasn't been said before? It does have great special effects, oh yes, but the acting is below sub par. The movie does not only suffer from actors merely reading from a script, but James Cameron seems to be 'borrowing' from other movies to make this uber movie in his image.

On with the good. Though I did not see this movie in theaters, my TV was good enough to view the visuals and be in awe of the scope of the planet of the Na'vi. From the local animals, to the vegetation to even some of the battle scenes, the special effects were top notch. I have no complaints about the movie from this respect. So, if you wish to see the movie based solely on special effects, see this movie without hesitation, and disregard the next part of my review.

Now the bad. First, the acting is less then spectacular compared with the effects that truly drive the movie. Sam Worthington, Sigourney Weaver, Michelle Rodriguez and even Giovanni Ribisi, all actors and actresses I like to watch and enjoy, were deadpan in this movie while delivering lines, trying to be emotional and even just interacting with one another. There's no chemistry with anybody, no character development, and no reason for us, the audience, to want to follow any of these individuals during their time on this planet out in the middle of nowhere. Had the actors been given better lines instead of tired, recycled, and predictable lines, then the movie might have been saved, but that isn't the case. The same goes with the Na'vi characters. And why is this? Because we've seen them before.

What I mean by this is these characters we see on screen, both "good" and "bad" are direct ripoffs of other movies that are heads over heels better then this movie. Ribisi is merely Burke from Aliens, Weaver is Sean Connery from Medicine Man, the Na'vi are the Native Americans from Dances with Wolves, Worthington is the soldier given a 'second chance' from countless movies to list, and so on. Really, you could take Wolves, cut and pace scenes from Aliens with Burke, have voice overs from Connery, throw in Tom Cruise's character from The Last Samuri and have fight scenes from Starship Troopers and a large dab of great special effects, and BAM, you have Avatar.

But that isn't what kills this movie. What really put the nail in the coffin for me was the pace and predictability of the film. I won't go into details, but there were times that screamed "Hey, we are mentioning this now early in the movie to be used later on to enhance a cool scene" that sadly did not disappoint. This is a classic 'paint by numbers' movie that showed little creativity.

If you're looking for a great movie with great action scenes and acting, go somewhere else. But if you wish to head to Na'vi and watch excellent special effects with terrible acting, then go ahead and put this movie in. But be warned...

title: Avatar - A New Beginning
review: Cameron wanted Avatar to release in 1999 but it was destined to release in 2009 and it created a wave of visual extravaganza. The story is embodied by the expert filmmaker, Cameron in a unique way by creating a never before seen world. As the movie ends you will feel like you have been brought back to planet earth, because when we are watching Avatar we are in Pandora. The plot of Avatar somewhat resembles with The Last Samurai and Dances with Wolves but it is a completely different ride in a magnificent world. Jake Sully is an ex-marine who lost his legs, to make a fresh start he arrives Pandora to join Military. The business of the military is to bring humans in contact with the Na'vis. The mission of military is to relocate the blue colored Na'vis so that humans can use the large deposit of valuable minerals. Colonel Quarich who runs the operation, ask Jake Sully to go under cover as a Na'vi, to learn the secrets of Pandora and to win their trust so that humans can take the advantage. Jake Sully is moved by the beauty of Pandora and his heart gets lost to the Na'vi princess Neytiri. The film thus turns to a kind of light hearted adventure story. His loyalty to the humans starts to turn when he feels that humans would ruin the world of Pandora. Will he fight for the blue side? The landscape of Pandora is the most creative and inventive of the decade. The creatures and plants you might find in your wildest dreams or your worst nightmares are beautifully shown in Avatar. Despite great visual effects of Avatar, creative world of Pandora and being latest in the film technology, Cameron uses typical old formula which works well. Avatar is one movie which will be known for years and it will also act as an inspiration for sci-fi genre movies.

title: Visually, the best film ever. Otherwise, still a great film.
review:
Back in 1997, visionary director James Cameron came out with the romantic drama Titanic, which won best picture of the year and became the biggest film of all time. 12 years later, Cameron comes back with Avatar, which is now the biggest film of all time.

I truly wish that The Dark knight, which is on the top 3, was the biggest movie of all time. But I can accept the fact that Avatar is. Avatar is gorgeous. You'll never see anything like it. It's truly a beautiful film.

When you watch this film, you are not expecting great acting. You are expecting awesome action sequences and special effects and not that good of a story plot. Well ,actually, the story plot is good. It's like Pocohontas but with blue alien like people. There are awesome action sequences and special effects. And the acting isn't bad.

Sigourney Weaver is actually quite humorous as the expert on the Avatar program. Stephen Lang does a really good job of getting on your nerves. Zoe Saldana does some ballsy acting and some talented acting too as an alien, and to some surprise I actually liked Sam Worthington. I originally thought that they were trying to turn him into the next Russell Crowe. Now I kind of understand why they are casting him. Though he's not a great actor, he isn't that bad.

Worthington plays Dr. Jake Sully, a wheelchaired man who is sent to do The Avatar program because he has the same DNA as his late brother. He goes into his Avatar and he meets a female alien(played by Zoe Saldana). She introduces him to her tribe and she begins to train him and they eventually fall for each other. All is well until the group Sully is with tries to destroy Pandora, which is what I forget to mention, is a beautiful jungle where the aliens live.

James Cameron is a film director that will spend billions and billions of dollars wisely. He has done it many times and has never failed. Some film directors will blow there money away(Michael Bay for Transformers 2). Some deserve to use it(Christopher Nolan).

Avatar is a fantastic motion picture event. It is perfect. The visuals are gorgeous, the film is kind of deep, the acting isn't bad, and just everything about it. The film is sad also. It did deserve to be nominated for best picture, though it wasn't my favorite film of the year. Avatar is a film that you can't miss out on. It's long, but so was Titanic. That was a great film ,and so is this.

Avatar:A+

title: Major Step Forward
review:
I didn't exactly know what all the hype was about before I actually saw Avatar at home on BluRay. Now I wished I had seen it in 3-D in a theatre. It is a technical tour de force. In a year that didn't really produce that many exciting films, I am somewhat at a loss to figure why it didn't win Best Picture. Politics I suppose or maybe something more Let's examine that.

What avatar isn't is a philosophically deep movie. A lot of people draw the obvious parallel to Dances With Wolves although Little Big Man also comes to mind. The characters herein are cardboard however, the plot utterly predictable from the opening scene. We are the ugly Americans, laying waste to everything we touch. One of our midst is sent out to destroy the enemy. He instead falls in love with them and ends up becoming one of them. Zzzzzzzzzzzzz. Been there seen that. It never hurts to be reminded that Mother Earth is herself alive nor that all creatures great and small deserve their rightful place as her children. Never hurts at all. So it's fine with me that in this worldview the buffalo finally get their revenge. 'Bout time. So what was accomplished? A lota whole lot.

Technically.

Notwithstanding that a new cogent universe was created, Cameron and crew advanced the art of film making an entire order of magnitude. The graphics are simply amazing. Fantasy takes on the cloak of reality here. The actors are empowered, not trivialized. Againthe term empowered is used in the technical sense; they are actually weakened by a hackneyed utterly predictable script. But can you imagine what these same actors, armed with a gifted writer behind them might achieve? That will be the true legacy of this film. That's why it deserved the Best Picture Oscar. No other film in the competition really had the juice of 'legacy'. What Cameron & Crew achieved will live on for years.

title: Visuals ten, script, etc. eight
review:
The eye candy in "Avatar" is admittedly gourmet in quality. I especially enjoyed those luminous Portuguese Men of War (Were Cameron's special effects people inspired by Disney's Fantasia?). However, Cameron himself was understandably afraid to carry the satire too far, lest there be less time and space for the action. The target is obviously the U.S.'s alleged tendency to muscle its way into oil producing countries, whatever the cost to the natives of those countries. But Cameron--or his writers--knew that the juvenile crowd (including those over thirty) could only take so much satire, so the action takes over big time, with an expendable heroic person knocked off, possibly to keep a few hankies damp. The film is formula right down the line: the confused and cynical hero who "learns" thanks to a courageous and wise female, the seemingly indestructible villain who mouths all sorts of funny-mean phrases you know he will eventually eat, the terminator-type gigantic, mobile armor, and of course the monsters inspired by the Jurassic Park dinosaurs.

Having said all that, I must add that I stuck it out to see what would happen, and I was only too happy to put my mind and critical sense into neutral for two and a half hours. The story is unoriginal, a melange of clichés from other sci-fi fantasies; however, the action had more than the usual hypnotic, suspenseful thrills.

title: Awesome sci-fi movie on interracial relations
review: The big hit of 2009. The leader of the "1 Billion Dollars" very exclusive movie group. The "Revolution" in 3D movies. The movie that enchanted the whole world. But is it all that we make it to be? Let's start from the very beginning. As you have probably heard "Avatar" is really an old project. James Cameron first thought of it in the 80's and he even managed to get in production, but he soon realized that the technology wasn't quite up to the task so it got postponed until it was finally done in 2008/2009. The concept of the story is quite complex. It's set in a future where Humans have reached far more than the boundaries of their own galaxy and discovered a planet called Pandora. This planet – Pandora – is inhabited by very different species, and the most similar to Humans is a species called " Navi' ". The Navi' are a people that co-inhabit and coexist with nature in pure harmony. They embrace it and let it embrace them through an inner network, which resembles our own system of neurons. But as awesome as that seems the Human's real objective there isn't to explore the planet. It's to exploit it and get a special mineral which sells at 25 million dollars a kilo. Yet it isn't as simple as just getting there and "reaping" it. The largest deposit is actually right under a gigantic tree which is the home of the Navi', since they live in its interior. As you can see, this setup of the story won't bring a happy ending for either side. So the Humans with all their fancy technology decided to create real bodies similar to the Navi' which they call avatar. The avatars are controlled by the Humans through a special connection and special machines. Jack, one of the protagonists by a twist of fate, is put in control of one of these avatars. The connection with the avatars is so strong that they feel everything just as one would feel in their own body. These avatars are capable of living in Pandora like a native of the planet itself. With the avatars the Humans plan not only to explore the planet but also to try and manipulate the Navi' to "move" from their Home Tree so that they can extract the mineral. Unfortunately even when they manage to fully "infiltrate" one of their avatars into the Navi' people all they got was a refusal. The Navi' consider the Human ignorant and their goals a rape to their planet, which they happen to love. Due to their acceptance of their planet, the Humans goals feel like murder and as such they refuse to participate or collaborate in any of that. So in an act of abuse of the very little trust the Navi' gave them, the Humans attacked and destroyed the Home Tree of the Navi'. This obviously resulted in war, but since the Navi' weren't exactly very technologically advanced – not that they needed anyway – the Humans very easily overpowered them. Jack, the "avatar" that became one of the Navi' betrayed the Humans and joined the fight for the Navi' side. To rally up the Navi' people he became Turok Makto and brought together the many, many tribes of Pandora, so that even if the Humans had more fire power they would have more "men" power. It still wasn't enough though. When the battle began it became evident that even with a much bigger army the Navi' would be decimated. When all hope was lost Pandora came to the rescue. Yes, you've read that right. Pandora. The animals joined and fought alongside the Navi' against the Humans and won the fight quite easily actually. After the fight ended the Humans were kicked out of Pandora for good and thanks to the connection between the Navi' and his avatar, Jack left his broken Human body and truly became a Navi' in the body of his avatar. Quite obviously there is much more to "Avatar" than just this, but I decided no tell it all so you could enjoy the marvelous movie by yourself. The acting, directing, the musical score, everything is amazing in "Avatar", even for those that aren't huge fans of the sci-fi genre. And the 3D makes the whole experience that more wonderful. (Luis Roque)

title: The Lion is Back to Roar Again.
review:
When all is said and done, when you look at Avatar as a movie apart from its social phenomenon, you are supposed to find this a parable for Western politics. Cameron clearly does. Indeed, implicating computer technology for its central role in man-made destruction, Avatar nevertheless utilizes the very same to create some of its innovative and hugely influential visuals. The bulk of Cameron's work displays an apparent distrust of technological advancement which is peculiarly at variance with his elaborate deployment of state-of-the-art cinematic technology. His post-Vietnam and post-feminist action epics---Aliens, the Terminator movies, True Lies---draw upon both technological and nuclear anxiety in the midst of Reagan's resurgent Cold War politics.

Avatar itself is fundamentally hailed for being a technological advancement. It is an exceedingly, outlandishly gigantic visual experience unlike anything we've seen before. It has an explicit Green and anti-war message. The writings on the wall dictate that it launch a worshipping faddism. It contains such visual embellishment that it surely sweetens repeated viewings. It even authors a new language to which I doubt human beings can do justice. It is the quintessential event movie, one of those films you feel you need to see to keep up with social discourse. Setting Napoleonic, Bond villain-esque humans against virtuous extraterrestrial rebels is a hopeful U-turn of the Aliens stencil, but perhaps requires Paul Verhoeven's keen comic-book intensity to drive the reversal into real subversion.

The human analogy on the lush, Earth-like moon of Pandora is a ten-foot-tall blue-skinned species of sentient humanoids called the Na'vi. An Earth corporation is mining a valuable mineral known with mystifying ambiguity as unobtanium. But for us humans to brave outside of our landing domain, we use avatars, Na'vi doppelgangers grown naturally and mind-controlled by humans who lay down wired up unconscious on the ship, which is where the 3-D element becomes more than just an ogling tool and takes on a metaphysical effect. While functioning as avatars, we sense and feel like Na'vi, and have all the same physical skill. The most interesting element of this is how the hero is a paraplegic. Rather than being a self-evident badass, he's been recruited since he's a genetic match for his dead twin brother, for whom an expensive avatar was constructed. In avatar state he is exhilarated by his magnified ability to walk again, not to mention being ten feet tall, and his compensation for this assignment he will be given a very expensive operation to recover movement in his legs. Theoretically he's good to go, for if his avatar is harmed, his human body is elsewhere.

The Na'vi survive in their world by having a deep relationship with it, living as one with nature, and being thoughtful about the creatures they share with. In this and various other ways they symbolize Native Americans. Like them, they discipline another species to have them at their disposal, like giant flying dragon-like creatures. On that admirable note, I found the significance tapering into impatience nearing its obligatory colossal climactic showdown between humans and aliens. After all a character has done that has betrayed the noble Na'vi, returning to them with a demonstration that he has tamed a supposedly untamable dragon-like super-creature, all is forgiven. It's just too sexy for them to stay mad anymore.

Indeed the bigger it all is, the cockier. Every bit of James Cameron's muscle seems to go into making our eyes bulge and genuflect in worship of the 3-D dazzle on the screen. On one hand, it's an outstandingly accessible exhibition of defying capitalism and championing the up-hill battle for the defense of nature, but done with mostly stale dialogue and boilerplate characterization. Essentially, it's a $237 million, 162-minute montage of cardboard allegories and plot devices, made by putting a bunch of screenplays in a blender. But we still say Wow! And why not? If you can get a theater full of people here in the American Midwest to flock to and cheer for America getting conquered by an indigenous tribe in war, then you've got one amazing work of spectacle. It's the experience, more than the allegory, that's worth a nod.

title: Avatar review
review:
Star date: May 4th, 2010 ;) Imd(i)b-er's log:

Let's say first that I am a newcomer on IMDb and, being French, I apologize for the quality of my English.

"Avatar", interesting title, isn't it? I wonder how they will call the next M. Night S. movie, knowing the tremendous critical and financial success that Iron Jim's movie had.

First, I saw this movie in December, when it was not yet clear if it will be the huge success we know today. I saw it in 2D and I must say I was disappointed. Unconsciously, I had compared this movie with another one that I saw the same week: 2012. The apocalyptic extravaganza touched me more, for I was more moved by the real characters in 2012 than the blue ones in Avatar.

Also, knowing the huge investment in Avatar movie, the epic scale, the groundbreaking 3D special effects etc, the only movie I could compare it was The Return of the King. They are two different genres, but still, I believe in a quality crux/core of the movies, no matter their genre. Once again, emotionally, I was not as impressed as I was on hobbits and nazguls ;).

What lacks to Avatar is a compelling and rich script. It is too predictable, and too linear in storytelling. Maybe, if you believe it is a documentary style film, it makes sense. Jim, where is the amazing script à la Terminator 2?

Also, I would have loved a less Manichean view on the bad guys. They had incredible technology and maybe interesting views and projects on Pandora. I wanted to see more... I can't believe they were only evil.

But, there is a twist in my story. After seeing it in 2D, two weeks later, I gave it a try in 3D. I had to do it because, being an unconditional Cameron's fan, I "forced" myself to love this movie ;).

The result was mesmerizing! The movie gained in shape and somehow in depth. I can't explain it to myself, but is seems that the 3D took off all the flaws, as it took me into the story till the end. Being also a pleasure for the eye (thanks also for the smooth pacing), one tend to forget the weaknesses of the script. It changes the movie and makes it so much better!

The 3D is amazing with perfect depth and CGI animation. Gollum, technically put, unfortunately, is far behind us... The performance and motion capture are used at their best! The creatures and the natives were great and with a rich culture. The conflict on Pandora somehow reminds me of Harry Harrison's "Deathworld".

But just some things about 3D. It would have been much better if:

-the creatures could pop-out the screen as they did in Ice Age 3 (it's more spectacular)

-they had used subjective view as they were flying . In 3D, again on Ice Age 3, I had the impression to literally flying. I had the same impression on Star Wars 3 in the opening scene, and it was only in 2D. So, it's even more breathtaking in 3D.

So: It will be cool having more subjective view + moving chairs and physical effects in movie theaters (like wind). But I am dreaming...:)

The music: I would expect better from M. Horner. On Aliens he was amazing! I mean, come on, we can hear a melody from his previous war movie in the beginning... If it only were for Brad Fiedel to do the music...

But all in all he did a good job, with "junglesque" score and epic dimension.

This movie should been taken as a whole experience, in order to be appreciated. It is, fore sure, the best extravaganza I have seen in long time!

I am a huge Sci-Fi movies fan, and I was waiting for a movie like this since Star Wars 3. Of course, there was District 9 which had a great script, but smaller in scale and epic action.

So, I will give a 9/10 to this movie, because it's breathtaking and ambitious. James Cameron is one director who will stay in shadow for 10 years and then do a master piece.

title: Worth the Experience
review:
First things first. Is Avatar deserving of the unrelenting hype? Its status as the highest grossing movie of all time? Could ANY movie truly live up to that billing? Probably not, but in terms of sheer scope of the visuals and storytelling, it is easy to see why James Cameron's Avatar became the phenomenon it is.

With a rumored budget of more than 300 million, there's never any question that the visual effects are the main star here. I might run out of adjectives rather quickly in going into detail why this movie is an easy 10/10 in the visual department. Comparisons with the original Star Wars are in this way warranted. Cameron has raised the bar on film-making in a lot of the same ways George Lucas did back in 1977. For perhaps the first time, I actually forgot I was watching CGI characters interact for most of the movie. The motion capturing was as close to perfect as I've seen. The environments were incredibly immersive. The colors were incredible. There was so much detail put into it, so much going on in the background, but it never overdid it in a way that movies such as the Star Wars prequels did. Cameron does understand the concept of letting a shot breathe. You might see critters or other such things in the background, but the shots never get distracting. It's definitely impressive how he created a whole world that lives before us, right down to the grass, plants, animals, and atmosphere. I could go on and on, but simply put, this movie looks freaking beautiful.

A lot has been said about the story. Yes, it's in no way original. Yes, it seems pieced together from other films. There's a lot of Dances With Wolves, there's some Ferngully style environmentalism, there's things I immediately recognized as being taken from The Matrix, Aliens and Star Wars. The lead in to the jungle areas of Pandora were just like the tour into Jurassic Park. But take a step back and consider: Is Dances with Wolves a better experience than Avatar? Is Ferngully presented in a way that's even half as effective? This film does aspire to be a classic like the other films mentioned, and I'm not convinced it's really so different, at least in terms of storytelling. Avatar lacks some of the heart in terms of the character development and personalities, but the overall story honestly didn't bother me at all. Sometimes taking a familiar concept can be OK as long as it's improved upon. It's a story we've heard before, but in this case the way it is presented never felt too forced or cliché for my taste. That being said, it's too bad it wasn't a bit more original. At least in Star Wars we had light sabers and the force and all that, the fact that Avatar lacks it's own spin in this way does hold it back from being a masterpiece.

The other issue I had with the story was that we seemed to join it midway in, with little explanation for the motivations of the characters based on what had happened before. This seems to be a deliberate decision by Cameron, and I'm not asking for flashbacks or anything, but there must have been a way to convey to the audience what was at stake a little better. Because of this, and the way the film spends the first 90 minutes basically showing us pretty pictures, the plot and characters don't really get truly engaging until the half way point. Around the time the romantic subplot kicked in, we were in full gear, and I had very few problems from this point on.

The cast in Avatar was a saving grace in my opinion. Sam Worthington was a good choice for the everyman main character, and Sigourney Weaver was a good choice as someone that has screen presence. Also, I was very happy to see Michelle Rodriguez and Joel Moore, as I've always been a fan of their supporting roles in the past. They nailed the casting across the board, which did a considerable job of making up for the otherwise less than fleshed out characters. There was a few moments of cheesy acting, but they did a good job with what they had to work with and succeeded at making me care about them by the end of the film.

There are many that thought Avatar was heavy handed in it's obvious messages. Knowing most of these going in, I was not bothered in the slightest. For a film with this long a running time, I was pleasantly surprised with how fast it went by. The pacing was done well and I was very thankful that the action didn't just drag on forever with no creativity put into it.

Avatar is quite the experience. It deserves to be seen by virtually anyone, and for that, it's hard to argue with the fact that there is a lot of hype around it. A few aspects hold the film back from achieving the masterpiece status that it tries for, but it's about as close as it gets in my eyes without crossing that line. If only for the innovation on display, and the way it plays as kind of a greatest hits if you will of many classic movies that I have loved my whole life.With the proper additional material this could easily rise above that, so I will eagerly keep my eyes on the extended version when the time comes. In the meantime, suffice to say you won't find me in the camp of people that won't continue to enjoy Avatar as a beautifully done adventure.

9/10

title: One of the best cinematic experiences ever.
review:
Sam Worthington plays Jake, a paraplegic ex-Marine who's sent to a distant moon to infiltrate an alien species, known as the Na'vi. Human kind has found a valuable mineral called unobtainium on this world. Jake is assigned to a scientific program headed by Grace Augustine played by Sigourney Weaver. The science team has focused on learning as much as possible about the Na'vi in order to benefit scientific knowledge. Augustine's research team is funded by a corporation that is on world to mine the unobtainium. The story continues with Jake learning of the indigenous species to gain a advantage for the corporation to collect all the unobtainium on world. Jakes motives alter as he becomes on with the Na'vi. Jakes motives completely alter and he becomes a defender of the Na'vi.

Numerous themes are at work in this picture. Imperialism, militarism, anti-patriotism, and civilization and race are just a few. The theme of belonging and adaptation is the most prevalent. This theme is the underlying backdrop for the entire movie. It creates the struggle and guides the outcome as the movie progresses. This theme has a lot in common with Final Fantasy: The Spirits Within (2001). However, Avatar is a far more engrossing and well made movie. The special effects of the movie where outstanding.

The effects actually where integrated into the story instead of being the story. The effects made this alien vista believable and an alien race identifiable to man. The 3D was done will. It added the ability to believe the movie without overpowering its message, only visual enjoyment is lost in the non-3D version.

The masterful use of camera angles to portray the alien landscapes was well done. A lot of attention was devoted to camera position and angle. This forethought helps direct the action from huge battle scenes to intimate conversation between two characters.

The use of lighting was also masterfully done. It brings the jungle alive at night and shows the enormity of the world during the day. The change of lighting helps portray the conviction of the Na'vi as well as define the world that they live in harmony with.

I found this movie to be a top not notch film. I highly recommend it to everyone with an imagination. This movie will long be remembered and become as a cinematography classic. The 3D, special effects, lighting, and camera position and angle all combine to brining this world alive. The plight of the Na'vi and the actions of Jake all mesh together to create a visually stunning and wonderful story.

title: Best Picture. Best Director. Really.
review:
Marine Corporal Jake Sully (Worthington) is drafted to become part of the Avatar Program on Pandora. He is put into a capsule and emerges on the planet as a 10 or 12-foot tall Navi native of Pandora, (but he is still in the capsule. See?). The US is there for a valuable mineral needed. The problem is the Navi are sitting on top of it and the US needs them to move so the US can mine it. Sully's job is to get the Navi to move.

I now know why Avatar didn't win Best Picture and Best Director. The Academy never saw the movie. They heard so much about it by word-of-mouth they felt like they had seen it. Then, Ms Bigelow and a S.W.A.T. Team captured the entire Academy in a room and wouldn't let them out until she had Best Picture and Best Director in a slam dunk for the Hurt Locker. Pretty sure it went something like that.

I didn't watch it in 3-D. But, this is a visual treat regardless of what dimension you watch it in. There are not worthy and adequate words to describe what you will see. You have never seen anything like the visuals in this movie. You will, as I did, rediscover the color Blue. Also, the CGI is absolutely spectacular. James Cameron, the Director, is truly a genius.

Yes, the first half is a visual feast for your eyes. In the second half, the real story starts and as you may suspect, a war breaks out. Unless I missed something in the beginning, I never once heard anyone talk about Negotiations between the US and the Navi. It's possible I missed that because the beginning went by so fast, I had the feeling someone assumed I knew about Pandora, the Navi, the Avatar Program, the hi-Tech equipment and the robotics. I didn't know what the word AVATAR meant. And, exactly where is Pandora? That word-of-mouth didn't reach me.

As soon as those 3-D TV sets become available and affordable I will get the 3-D glasses and give this another go.

Oh, this is a movie you may want to buy, but wait. Wait until some time goes by and another copy will come out telling you this one includes deleted scenes or scenes never seen before. That's the one you want to purchase.
