title: Avatar, revealing what we try so hard to deny; An Amarican Palestinian's take on the movie.
review:
I was watching Avatar when Selfridge said "This is why we're here, because this little gray rock sells for twenty million a kilo" and latter Jake talks about how we turn innocents into terrorists when they have something we want, to give ourselves an excuse to fight them, and I look at my friend and say "so many movies have talked about that same exact thing, how can people still not know the truth, or at least doubt it?". Avatar may be a fictional fantasized movie but it mentions a reality as real as anything else.

In Avatar, the humans are manipulated by their leaders into fighting the Na'vis, thinking they are fighting terrorists, because the Na'vis' village lies on the riches deposit of the valuable stones the humans want. They forget that Pandora is the Na'vis' home and that they're the invaders. Though the Na'vis are overpowered by the humans' advance technology and warfare they show great bravery by standing up to defend what is rightfully theirs; they fight gunship with bows and arrows under Jake's inspiring words "They've sent us a message that they can take whatever they want. Well, we will send them a message, that this is our land!". As I watched the humans destroy Pandora and then the Na'vis kill the humans, I couldn't help feeling sorry for both. Both sides were victims, both didn't deserve their fate. The Na'vis were left no other choice, they had to fight and kill the humans before they themselves were destroyed and the humans were manipulated by their leaders into thinking they were doing a patriotic act, into believing they were fighting evil. Innocent men, human beings lost their lives in vein, killing innocent Men, Woman, Children and destroying their home land.

The reason I personally love this movie is that it hits so close to home, and inside it I see the real world portrayed in symbolic characters for those who refuse to see it in reality. American Men and women; fathers, mothers, sons, daughters, brothers, and sisters were manipulated into fighting in Iraq, they were told that they were fighting terror and freeing an oppressed people. Those patriotic soldiers believed their leaders and fought Iraqis in Iraq, killing the people and destroying the country. Today, the real aims of that war are clear and it is evident that the main purpose was oil and natural resources. It's like this in many places around the world. Always, leaders of powerful nations find riches; land, oil, gas, gold..etc, in weaker countries and send their soldiers to fight for it, those men go proudly under the delusion that they are patriots fighting terror. And always, innocents on both sides are killed.

In Avatar Jake says, "all I ever wanted was a battle worth fighting for", and then he finds one when he takes the Na'vis side in fighting the humans. It's ironic how we can relate to Jake, how we understand that the Na'vis' battle was one worth fighting for because they were fighting the foreign occupier of their land yet, we can call the Na'vis of the real world; the Iraqis, Palestinians, Lebanese and the others oppressed, terrorists when they do exactly the same thing as Jake and his Na'vi friends.

In the real world, there are good people who try to fight for peace, ignorant people who believe media propaganda and evil leaders who, driven by greed, murder and destroy countries afar. It's just like that in Avatar; "I dreamed I was a soldier who could bring peace. But eventually, you always have to wake up", says Jake representing the good people of the world, who dream of peace but are dismayed by the power of evil and its ignorant supporters.

This fictional movie enciphers so many truths about the real world, maybe I'm scrutinizing too much and going to deep when it was only meant for its superficial meaning. Fortunately though, whether the movie was meant for it or not, I am not alone in my extra analysis; as I was walking out of the theater this lady tells her husband "it's just like the Americans in Iraq" and I look at my friend with a witty laugh who says "she has your same theory".

title: Spectacularly Packaged Mindless Entertainment
review:
This film could be described as the "Star Wars" of its generation. This is a good news/bad news situation. Like the original 1977 "Star Wars" movie, it is a high-spirited, breathtaking feast of cutting-edge special effects. In the present case, the level of detail of the computer animation is astonishing, both in the backgrounds and in the animated humanoid aliens; the expressive flaws that dogged earlier efforts such as "Beowulf", especially in the eyes, have been solved. In this respect, the film has set a new standard. (It is also being widely shown in a stereoscopic (3D) form; it is claimed that this 103-year-old technology has finally gone mainstream in cinema. That remains to be seen; we've heard that before.) But just as the original "Star Wars" hangs its special effects extravaganza on a lame, hackneyed comic-strip of a plot, so similar problems dog "Avatar"; an intellectual, thought-provoking movie this is not. The premise is that a paraplegic Marine from a dead, despoiled home world accepts a posting as a mercenary on the idyllic forest world of Pandora, in a mission to convince the blue humanoid natives to abandon their territory so that the rapacious Company can mine it for precious deposits of "unobtainium" (LOL), whose value is never even explained to the viewer. The protagonist is to act as ambassador to these natives by mind-linking to an alien body called an avatar and piloting it through the Pandoran forest to interact with the natives.

In defter hands something interesting might have been made of this, but what we get is a stale mishmash of themes from "Ferngully", "Dinotopia", "George of the Jungle" and "Dances with Wolves",without even the winsome charm of some of those films. The plot is painfully predictable: the hero goes rogue and rebels against his corporate overlords to take the natives' side;there is the obligatory climactic battle between the good guys and the bad guys; the characters (other than Sigourney Weaver's quirky Dr. Augustine) are cardboard cutouts; there are numerous illogicalities in the film's premises; and there is nary a surprise or plot twist anywhere to be found.

So just turn your brain, off kick back, enjoy the show, and don't bother to think too much about it afterwards.

title: Why bother?
review:
Why bother spending years and hundreds of millions of dollars making a movie, if you're not going to tell a story that hasn't been told before? The story in this film has been told thousands of times before, and it's been told thousands of times better.

Even with all of the opportunities for doing something different that were presented by the technology and the subject matter, we still get a movie where the helpless natives are saved by the "chosen one" in the form of a white, American Marine.

If you're looking for eye candy, this film will give you all you could ever want. If you're looking for a great story for the 21st century, look elsewhere.

title: Good Movie, But Not The Great Triumph That You Hear About
review:
With all the hype, "Avatar" had a lot to live up to. I thought it was a really great film, but it did not live up to all the hype for me. It would be one thing if it was the first 3D movie experience, but I saw "A Christmas Carol" just two months earlier and knew what to expect on that front.

The look of "Avatar" is very cool. The landscapes are all wonderful to look at and with the all the glow-in-the-dark surroundings paired with the 3D environment it really made me feel as though I was in an attraction at Disney World rather than in a movie theater.

The concept was pretty cool as well. I liked the fact that Jake lived these dual lives. It seems like careful planning would have to be taken when that sort of thing is to be achieved and it was done quite seamlessly here.

As for the story goes, I thought it was okay. It reminded me a lot of "The Last Samurai", only not done as well. The way that the enemy of the natives is taken in and then grows to love and belong to the civilization that he was once out to destroy. "The Last Samurai" ends much better than this though. Here it is very predictable that the good guys will win, Jake gets to become one of them and gets the girl, and the humans are shipped home while nature prevails.

A small nitpick that I have with this film is the year that it takes place in. 2154? So 144 years in the future the human race will develop all this new technology, discover an new planet in a new solar system, travel to it, and begin living and colonizing there? James Cameron really has a lot of faith in science and technology flourishing quickly.

title: Pretty but lacking substance
review: Firstly let me state that Avatar is not as 'bad' a film as some people make it out to be. That said neither is it a good film. Avatar is a leap forward in graphics but sadly not in any other area. The CGI is spectacular CGI. It does not create realism however, it creates a very good CGI world. What I am saying here is that you are constantly aware of the CGI environment and, sorry if I sound old fashioned here, but isn't suspension of disbelief a fundamental part of cinema viewing? the charm and unique nature of Avatar is its technology and you must accept that this film for what it is before condemning or praising it too hard. Take out the clever CGI (which time and familiarity will do as it does with all effects based films) and you are left with a rather preachy movie that has some very juvenile and often clunky dialogue. The 'we are all one with our planet' message is rammed down our throats so much that I began to feel preached at by a giant smurf, and as I watching it in 3D he kept leaning into my popcorn to do it. Don't expect too much, accept Avatar as a glorified Saturday morning keep the kids quiet film and it works just fine.

title: Great eye candy, too bad about the plot
review:
The movie was beautiful! Utterly breathtaking.

The plot was a fine familiar old story set in a new context.

!!!Spoiler alert

I was with the story all the way up to the battle. That battle, the way it was fought and won undermined if not obviated a key theme in the story; that ignorance is a weakness.

The natives of the planet had this profound connection with the planet and definitively meager weapons. Yet when composing a strategy to go up against the heavily militarized opponent they chose a very direct head to head/charge of the light brigade approach, and were subsequently slaughtered. Granted they were victorious but only by the providence of of a god.

I thought the film would have been a lot more compelling if the lead character had composed a strategy that took into account the natives unique capacities and his unique knowledge of the humans' approach and weaponry. Had he done so he would have demonstrated the power of knowledge. the natives' victory would have occurred with significantly less loss on both sides. Seems to me that that outcome would be more in keeping with the manner of this new being he had become and the world he was trying to preserve.

For instance, the weaponry of the human force was hobbled by the weird magnetic fields of that area, but the natives were wired into this huge world brain that senses everything. Did the natives use that to their advantage by leading the enemy onto itself, no.

I once heard that the defining characteristic of science fiction is that the science, the unique technology, etc plays a role in the plot. This had the potential to be that but instead it was just the same old fairy tale about a civilized man being reborn when he goes native. *yawn*

Nice graphics though. You should peal off .05% of that CG budget and hire a few writers next time. Or perhaps it was just written to a perceived audience. The one that somehow needs to reconcile a tale about conservation, tolerance and respect with the manner of a society that will employ military force to exploit and even destroy resources, cultures, and even species all for sake if short term profit.

title: Overinflated balloon popped.
review: Why on earth don't they spend more time on the spot rather than spending more money on the movie? The end is so obvious from the beginning. Graceful tree-hugging Na'vis vs. greedy human-beings. So beyond LOTR or Matrix even though how much hi-tech is involved. What a waste of fiscal sources invested in! I respect the endeavor. But I didn't like it. It was the most emotional and educational video game I've ever seen. Promotion - Marketing - Trade. Mr. Cameron is richer than yesterday, since he taught us a good lesson? I was expecting a good plot, but all I got was strong visuals. It is not enough. At least, the film doesn't deserve the praises it got. When the praises were so overstated, my expectations got higher. Overinflated balloon popped. Characters imitated from Matrix or LOTR. Sully is so like Neo, rebellious, ignorant at first, then he crosses the good side and falls in love. An oracle who reads the marks. "Elf"ish kingdom; they respect the nature, they are noble and they are supernatural. Oh please. It's lacking the originality on every plane. Before the movie, there was a huge sequence of commercials. Some of them were about Wii games. I find them more original in terms of technology.

title: Superb Special Effects / Boring Childish Story
review:
To cut a big story short:

Special Effects: 10 Stars

Story: 4 Stars

I was amazed with the special effects. Watching this movie on 3D was an absolutely crazy and impressive experience. I was delighted. I was so delighted that I simply forgot how average sticky the story was, totally predictable and really uninteresting. But the effects, WOW!

As a friend of mine told me while we were watching the movie: "Fuck the story!"

Don't miss this new movie experience.

title: My neck hurts, but: What a movie!
review:
Going into the theater, I didn't put too much hope into this film. Even though I love pretty much all of Cameron's work (with the exception of, maybe, Piranha II), these days you can't take the quality of a movie for granted just because a big director is at the helm. Just look at the Star Wars prequels or Indy 4.

I saw Avatar on one of the biggest screens in my hometown on X-Mas-day, it was pretty much sold out and I could only get a very bad seat: first seat in row four..ouch! But you know what? Once the film started, I hardly noticed the uncomfortable viewing-position. This alone and the fact that I also hardly noticed the 160-min running time speak volumes for the quality of the film. It's been a long time since I've seen such a strange, beautiful, "realistic" and fantastic world brought to life so perfectly on the screen. It really puts Lucas and his Star Wars prequels to shame.

And yet: Even though I know that 60% of the action is CGI, I never lost my suspension of disbelief. The creatures look so life-like, the blend between real actors and computer-graphics is so seamless that it never distracts you. Granted: The story is pretty much a rehash of Last Samurai/Dances with Wolves, even down to details such as the love-story or certain characters' fates. But so what? The love-story itself should be old news ever since Shakespeare's Romeo + Juliet, but good variations of the theme still can cut it in our modern age. So does Avatar: Cameron shows once again why effect-fests like Transformers simply don't work: If you don't have a good story and likable, fleshed-out characters you can throw in all that CG-crap you want: The film's not gonna draw you in. Effects should always be used as a means to tell your story, to enhance your vision. And even though Avatar is full of some of the most amazing CGI I've ever seen, Cameron uses it just as that: as a film-making tool, albeit, a very powerful one.

Before this gets too long, let me close by highly recommending that you watch Avatar in 3D. The process works amazingly well, is used pretty subtly here and there wasn't a single shot that felt like they were just showing off the 3D-capabilities. If you've seen "Jaws 3D", you know what kind of shots I'm talking about.

title: over-hyped movie
review: I agree, The CGI were detailed and hi tech, But reading other reviews on this movie, I thought it must be a groundbreaking thing that will move me to the core and I would see cinema with a different set of eyes!! I personally do not think it came anywhere close to Titanic or jurassic park which when I first saw, threw me completely, had seen nothing like it ever. I happened to watch it in Imax 3D and I seriously think people need to wake up and stop denying that it was the years most over-hyped movie. james camerons titanic had a soul, a story that tugged at your heart and the effects were just a bonus to the overall experience, but this movie does not have any emotions, both jake/grace or even the villain do not seem convincing enough to fight to death for their cause, I think a little build up would have helped. Three hours of graphics and nowhere did I feel my heart pulled at or anything, I think the story was predictable and graphics over the top. I think apocalypto is a much better ride if you want a REAL movie and not some digitalized version of alien/planet of the apes reruns.

title: Great effects, BUT ...
review:
Avatar is an interesting movie. On one hand, we got a strange new world, full of unusual, yet strangely compelling creatures, all conjured up in front of our eyes. It's filled with mystique and awe. It's what is currently dazzling the crowds and it's an aspect of Avatar that will likely win it several more awards, which the movie well deserves.

On the other hand, if you look beyond the visual effects, you will find a worn-out and utterly predictable plot, static characters with personalities as deep as a teaspoon and dialogs resembling an average daily commute: a necessary evil, that serves it's purpose and slips into obscurity immediately afterward. The entire 2 hours and 41 minutes of the movie does not contain a single surprising turn of events, a single character doing something we wouldn't expect him or her to do shorty after initial introduction and, most painfully, not even a single memorable spoken line.

The movie is worth seeing for the special effects - go watch it in 3-D to get most out of it. It can be quite enjoyable, if you immerse yourself into the world and ignore everything else. Don't expect a film of the year, however, that's just a hype. It's more of a postcard of another world, with some events happening in it.

title: Not a benchmark film
review:
I was looking forward to Avatar. I saw it on the second day it played and paid the extra money for the 3D. I enjoyed it, but it's far from the benchmark film some have been claiming.

First the motion-capture technology is fine when used to replicate body motion, but not facial expressions. It can duplicate basic broad facial movements, such as anger or laughter, but anything subtle is simply not there. You still relate to the alien characters as being animated and the earth characters as being real actors. We're obviously expected to not be aware of any difference between animated characters and real actors, but there is a substantial difference.

There is also a huge lack of original ideas for both technology and the creatures inhabiting the planet. Star Wars, Alien, 2001 A Space Odyssey or even going back to Fantastic Planet, gave the public technology and environments which had never been seen on the movie screen before. It's not that these films were absolutely original as they did borrow ideas. But when they did borrow, for the most part, they were not from other films and so it was new to the general public. Avatar just borrows too heavily from other movies we've all seen. For heaven's sake, did the bad guy REALLY have to get into one of those giant robotic suits for the climactic battle? Technologically, there is nothing in here that compares to the first time the public saw the space station wheel in 2001, or the H.R. Giger sets of Alien, or the giant planet walkers in Star Wars. Then there are the animals which inhabit the planet which look far too similar to earth animals. Basically, the alien tigers look like tigers and even the dinosaur-like creatures, well, look like dinosaurs!

And the action scenes, somehow didn't generate the excitement they should have. For example, when they were flying on the backs of the giant bird-creatures, I never felt the particularly thrilled by it. A flying scene like that should have made you feel a sensation of vertigo. I was thinking that it might have been because the jungle environment was so strange and foreign that you had no sense of height the way you would in a city scene when buildings give your mind something to relate to. But I think there may have been a bigger reason. Greater importance was given to hammering home the message of the film, rather than simply being caught up in the action. So, flying on the backs of the birds was to show "the majesty of the natural world" instead of just the thrill of it. And the battle scenes were not the battle scenes in a Star Wars film, because it simply more important to feel the sorrow and horror of war. Compare the actions scenes in Avatar to Dark Knight and there is no comparison.

The only place Avatar excels is in the depth and detail of the planet. The jungle is probably the star of the movie. However, I could just go to an Imax showing of the real Amazon jungle and get the same experience.

If you keep your expectations reasonable, you'll probably enjoy Avatar. But this isn't the new Star Wars.

title: avatar is neytiri
review:
The CGI was great (of course), but I have seen that in pixar movies. Motion capture? Yes it is mind blowing in pixar movies too. The story? of course avatar is no where near pixar movies (except the cars of course).

May be it is my fault comparing avatar to pixar movies. But I definitely rate avatar above any of pixar movies released till date just because of the character neytiri played (or developed whatever) by the beautiful zoe saldana. Other characters such as jake avatarized beautifully by Sam Worthington comes only seconds to neytiri because zoe (oops neytiri!!) looks more human than any other character in the movie. She is an environmentalist a lover, a warrior.. a Na'vi with a human girl's heart (though very few girls have that kind of heart nowadays!!).

I love neytiri because,

1. She fell in love with a man from another race and she accepted it.

(Accepting something that your "traditional" mind may not be fully

comfortable with is called courage)

2. She was ready to obey her elders to teach a person from another race

(I bet she would have done that even if she hate him)

3. She risks her life for her love, and her race.

4. She puts her people above her love interest (the scene when she

finds out that "this" would happen.)

Overall neytiri is the simplest adaptation of a pure human heart and I love it.

title: More fantasy than good sci-fi
review:
All the special effects money can buy cannot override a soulless script. It exemplifies why the French consider American films sophomoric and vacuous. The same story could be sold to a Saturday morning, cartoon show for the infantile. Maybe it was intended just for kids.

The effects were great, but the sci-fi elements were mostly mere fantasy. Pandora is a moon-planet apparently in orbit around a Jupiter-like planet which can only mean substantial time in pitch black darkness. Didn't Cameron consult anyone knowledgeable in science? It looks pretty to the eye but it embarrasses reason. Since so much attention to detail was shown regarding the technology used to project the neurological soul to an avatar, why any less detail given to celestial mechanics?

Nonetheless, the beginning scene depicting hyper-sleep technology almost caused a lost of bowel control, it was so awesome.

A Man Called Horse is a far better story of whitey eventually recognizing the far, far, far, far, far nobler characteristics of indigenous people. Maybe Avatar is today's representation of that idea. If so, it sure cost a lot more to get the same idea across.

The ceremonial dance by the natives reminded me of a MGM musical. About 2 hours into the film I closed my eyes for a short break.

title: Think of it as getting an "experience" - not just seeing a movie.
review:
There are three things you should know about this movie: (1) See it in the theater in 3D if you can (and IMAX 3D if you have the opportunity) (2) DO NOT BE LATE - there were no previews at my showing, so folks who were in the concession stands when the lights went down missed the beginning of the movie and (3) be ready for a long movie - it's 2:40 minutes.

OK - I'll make this quick. Avatar is definitely worth seeing, but the greatest enjoyment you'll get from seeing it is from experiencing the fantasy world of "Pandora" - not from traditional movie elements like performances, plot, dialog, themes, etc. Of course, those are all there and they are very well done, it's just that they're not what makes this movie great.

Being exposed to a spectacular alien landscape with vivid colors, 3-dimensional perspective, fantastical creatures big and small, intricately detailed imagery and exotic locations is a large part of what this movie is all about.

If the visuals of the movie were any less strong or the acting/script/etc. were not strong enough to support the world Cameron created, the movie could easily have been a disaster.

I strongly recommend watching this in the theater because after watching the previews on TV, you're definitely going to lose a lot of the ambiance and atmosphere by watching it on a small screen. I plan to see it in the theater again.

title: spectacular but mediocre
review:
The visual effects are impressive and ground breaking, but the story is ho hum. Scout goes native after immersion in their ways - leading to the ultimate conflict of loyalties and rebellion from father figure. Etc.

Also, the big, "I Luv You This Much" eyes of the Nav'i, oi.

But overall, as with previous Cameron outings starting with Terminator, the details are very well coordinated and plausible. The low gravity and the magnetic flux fields etc. explain/account for a lot of weirdness (giant size creatures, floating rocks, etc.).

The only disconnect is at the end - no explanation of why kicking the current crop of humans off the planet would avoid their return in force. If the Unobtainium was so precious/vital/rare, then one would expect it would not be given up that easy. Some kind of explanation of a negotiated agreement would have been good.

Sequel opening, mayhaps? Nav'i learn human technology just in time to repel return attack? As with all technical advances, this virtual world technology will need a much stronger story to really show it's power.

title: Foster's Midworld?
review:
The movie is too closely based on Alan Dean Foster's Midworld. Parallels are in the terms: Home Tree and Sky People, the concepts of evolved adaptive humanoids (the native people), of "emfolling", and of an interconnected world mind. The local tribe shown here is much bigger that Earth's humans but essentially human nonetheless. The local tribe in Avatar places importance in the ritual of recognizing the sacrifice of a hunted and killed creature. The same concept is found in "emfolling" (emphatic foliation) in Midworld. The minds of pre-existing beings are merged with the Home Tree in Midworld, ditto in Avatar. The Invaders come from the sky and are dependent on high-technology in both Midworld and Avatar. The guileless introduction of sky people into the local culture is the same in both movies.

This is not to say that the adaptation was not in itself a very clever and very original work. I loved it. But credit should be given where credit is due.

title: the kids must have loved it...
review:
Well there is a lot to say about Avatar. When I first hear about it.. well since then I expected that I will see some cool SF movie with an outstanding story and excellent characters.. but.. well the movie started and the movie ended and I still don't know anything about the scenario and the world Avatar tried to illustrate. There were huge gaps in the story.. everything jumped from an action to another with no apparent reason.

We don't know what they do with unobtanium (who came up with this name anyhow?.. lack of imagination).. they don't even seem to care since they are ready to blow everything up around it. Why did they choose avatars to relate with the Na'vi instead of just going there themselves? How come they are still using wheelchairs, and why they use a heavy transport ship to carry the bomb on pellets.. after all, the rockets from the helicopters obviously worked on the big tree, why not on the glowing one as well? Why would they commit everything in one big push ? Then for the world.. How come you can find on Pandora only like 5 species of animals and some flying glowing seeds. I mean if they bothered to show the nature so much.. you'd expect..i dunno .. a bug? some rodents? flying insects?.. but no.. there's a panther, a bigger panther with another pair of legs, a triceratops, a big strange bird, and an even bigger strange bird... and the horse.. and they are all ridable.

Why would you build separately a big gun for the big robot instead of attaching it to the robot?.. maybe then they wouldn't have to build a big knife for the robot to fight with when he looses the gun. The reason for this is that the whole world was inspired from video games. I think Cameron kidnapped a few koreans for this movie.. Everything from floating mountains, ridable big birds, avatars, those robots driven by humans.. everything looks very similar to things from recent video games (if you're a gamer this is very obvious). I think Cameron spent the last 15 years playing video games and this is what he came up with.

Characters - very boring, plain characters.. always speaking in clichés. I don't think any character from this movie will be long remembered. I barely remembered a couple at the end of the movie. The actors also didn't perform that well.

Now to be honest it's not as bad that it should get 1 out of 10.. but when I saw that many others rated it 10/10.. I couldn't think anything else than give the lowest rating to bring it down a bit. It's a fair 4/10.. has good graphics, pleasant to watch. So if you're not looking for a mind experience, but just an eye experience .. Avatar is great for you.

PS: they should be happy they got 3 Oscars.. each at a cost of 200.000.000$ tho :D

title: Flashing lights and loud things entertaining small minds
review:
A 10 year old would be ashamed of this script, so James Cameron - Shame on you! Those under 15 shouldn't mind, and will definitely love this movie. The novelty of the special effects will wear off quickly for many considering Avatars length, 162 minutes, on repeat viewings.

How on another planet we can't get on with each other - let alone the natives - yet are able to do so on Earth in order to build spaceships? There is no F'in way!!

I'm of the opinion that the Universe holds incredible wonders and riches beyond imagination. And I had hoped this movie would do that concept justice! Instead it chose to wallow in the mud of brainless ignorance pouring from every beautiful frame.

I went to see Avatar to experience a story set in a fantastic environment, instead I got to see said environment blown to smithereens without the story! And for me that isn't entertainment, in the same way the clubbing to death of the fur seal pups in Canada isn't!

It was never explained why the Humans didn't land as close as possible to the ideal mining location, and build a tunnel? It had to be cheaper than using/bringing all that military stuff. As well as the mining equipment we never did get to see?

title: Cameron's new film ultimately falls ironically flat despite 3D
review:
Seeing all these positive votes is a surprise to me. I genuinely believe this movie profits from the relative newness of 3D cinema effects. People are wowed by the beautiful renderings of nature, the RDA equipment and the Na'vi liveliness; I had to convince myself that these were all CGI. We've come a long way since Jar Jar Binks.

I too was impressed then, from the moment opening scenes touched my eyes through the lens of truth (the goggles), with scenery and characters seemingly popping out of the screen. After a while though, your grip on reality pulls you back, much like how this occurs with our human lead Jake Sully time and time again. See, the showing lasts more than 2.5 hours and during that long long time on a planet far far away, this effect alone failed to grip this viewer. I'd say the first half of the film is good, not on par with Cameron's older releases, but it creates a base for trust that all is going to be well with this movie. Then after about 90 minutes, the story just gets boring, with spectacle over substance taking over. The thing is, for a movie that doesn't require any thinking, it's just too long and ultimately uninteresting.

The tribal Na'vi are so incredibly goody good and in touch with nature in their tribal hippie ways it's almost sickening, while the RDA side takes the cake in showing off humans as a bunch of heartless corporate military types that only like flamethrowers, Mechs, bulldozers and blowing up large Mana trees. The black and white (or is it digital) nature of the two "teams" therefore is insignificant. I felt myself neither siding with the RDA (the side branded the enemy by the script) because of their horrible nature, nor with the Na'vi simply because the whole semi-helpless but prevailing native/tribal/aboriginal premise made me feel slightly embarrassed, nauseous and fatigued. The two sides offer no help in keeping you immersed due to their lack of identifiable content; neither are like "real people". The 3D effects are left to do that, but in the end the flat characterisation made me "wake up" from the dream about an hour into the movie and never sucked me in again after that.

It's a shame, but Avatar, as a consequence of its cheesy cliché ridden script (just tick mental boxes of "influential" source material for fun if you get bored at some point) and heavily dualistic right/wrong nature finds no opportunity to surprise the audience with any real feeling of care for what's happening to any of the leads, and more importantly it fails to let the viewer make a conscious choice who to root for. This is not T2 where you felt bad when Arnie sunk in the "lavapit", or, if you're a girl, this is not T where you felt bad when Leonardo sunk in "icewaterpit" (an ironic similarity there). This movie and the persona's fates all left me rather emotionless, save for the impact of the grand vista's and mesmerising effects.

With the director and writer deciding everything and the plot being more than obvious in its flow, Avatar ended up being underwhelming as a story, however brilliant as a tech demo. I say again, we will probably look back on Avatar in later years as one of the pioneers to widely distribute 3D tech and it deserves that place, but long before that the story will be forgotten and that cannot be said for films like Titanic, Aliens and Terminator 2, that managed to push the boundaries of technology, while also providing a story and characters that are worth caring about and remembering. So, why still 7/10? Well, despite the bland characters the movie is entertaining enough if you persevere and whichever way you look at it, it's a technological landmark that merits a good score, if only for a little while. But next time, Cameron, it's gotta have more cow bell.

title: Pretty Effects, Long Movie
review: My advice to you is where something comfortable when viewing Avatar. I would suggest a good pair of shorts, a snuggie, a dress, or a good pair of lose fitting pants. Man, my balls were hurting big time mid way thru the movie. I saw the movie at an IMAX theater in Anaheim, CA. I was surprised the projected film did not occupy the entire IMAX screen. There black bars on the left and right side of the rather small IMAX screen. I digress though, back to the movie. I stopped enjoying the special effects when Cameron decided to make a big deal out of the death Sigorney Weaver's character in the movie. It just dragged on and on. I think if the movie was pared down to under 2 hours, it would have been more enjoyable and less painful on the ball sack. Oh don't take any kids either, I saw a man take his 4 year old to a 10:40PM viewing, poor kid was scared.

title: What good is a movie with a great technology if it holds an average script?
review:
I must apologize if i mentioned AVERAGE here but after having high hopes on this movie, AVERAGE is the word i get. James Cameron is a film maker who is known for Titanic and Terminator 2 though he gave great action flicks like Rambo, True Lies and Aliens. He is a film maker known for great Visual effects. Of course Titanic had brilliant visual effects. It was so real that we didn't noticed the use of it. And now here again, this movie holds the greatest of the technologies. But wait, didn't we had this same technology in king kong, lord of the rings(gollum). Yes. But here Cameron has tried to use the same technology more meaningfully - Now script writers could think widen, come up with more imagination. Cameron has proved that every imagination could be given life. No kiddy animations anymore.

Now what is this great technology? Its the use of CGI characters. Not so long back, film makers used visual effects and graphic technologies to animate characters. Its the same here but there is one huge difference. Previously animators were used to move every single physical movement, facial emotion, speech and wrinkles using software. But here real actors were involved to make physical movements and facial emotions. Its called the motion capture technology where an actor's movements are translated digitally. Also the facial expressions and the finger movements which is known as performance capture. The actors wear markers in the face and the body joints to reflect every micro movement digitally and graphically. Thus, giving life to the imaginary CGI characters.

The movie majorly involves a species called Na'vi and their World - Pandora. The Government along with the army is in process learning Pandora and access its resources. Sam wothington who is paralyzed waist down participates in the Avatar Program which lets him control a genetically developed Navi(A Pandora Species) body. As a Navi, he inhabits with the Pandora and analyzes their world. In this process he starts loving the Pandora and their species and finally fights for their race against the human. Well doesn't it feels like Matrix meets District 9. Whatever, the screenplay is not so good - at least from this great film maker.

Its a great concept to present a visual treat. Like Cameron's previous movies this movie will shine for its visual effects. All this movie holds is for its visual effects. You couldn't feel even a single glitch. Bravo! The use of CGI characters is a real necessity of the film or the so called script. This movie is almost pictured using the CGI Characters.You see an imaginary species showing perfect emotions that an animation couldn't present.

Sam worthington was good. Real good. He has a good future after Terminator and Avatar. Other actors were also good. Especially the one that played the Navis.The Navis physical appearance has been designed so good that they look real and good. Especially good in emotional scenes. All the actors who were used for the CGI has done a wonderful job. To mention, the facial expressions were presented so real that the emotional scenes felt good. Background Music is good. 3D could have been used better. 3D just feels ordinary. IMAX could be better

The final 40 minutes is good. Its all about breathtaking action. And here we are talking about the guy who made big action Blockbusters like True Lies and Terminator 2. Supposed to be good.

Although there was a lack of good script, Cameron has given a good start for the futuristic film makers- the use of CGI characters. Now we could see great fiction movies that will look real. Forget the animations. Its old age now. Thanks to the great Cameron.

So just a good time pass movie. But that ain't James Cameron. And that ain't we expected.

title: Its ALL about the special effects
review:
I had high hopes for this movie, but like so many of my friends warned me, it really was Fern Gully with better special effects.

The effects themselves were gorgeous- seamless, detailed, fascinating to watch. Amazing colours and good use of the 3D. I'm not sure about being 'revolutionary' but it definitely sets a new standard in the progression of special effects.

There were, however, so many aspects that just let the film down. The music, by James Horner, was so ridiculously similar in composition to the theme from Titanic it was hard to not to laugh! The script was OK, nothing particularly brilliant but not out of place. Sam Worthington, though easy on the eyes, failed to grab audience attention and his constant accent slips were somewhat irritating, though not as pronounced as his performance in Terminator Salvation. Zoe Saldana, though always in motion capture form, stole the entire film from Worthington.

The plot was predictable and absolutely no part got my heart pumping. I was extremely let down by the (expected) death of the bad guy, which in all seriousness was completely comical.

It was definitely a beautiful, pretty movie, but Cameron may have done well to invest more across the board instead of just on the effects.

title: Bedknobs and Broomsticks
review:
It may have been a breakthrough in film-making, but this was not the breakthrough in film watching I was expecting. The CGI effects are no more convincing at mixing humans and animation than Bedknobs and Broomsticks or Mary Poppins. Closeup motion-capture for acting and some action is good, but obviously pure CGI animation for jumping, running and climbing still fails to convince. James Horner's over-familiar music covers this film like a really bad case of psoriasis. And Sam Worthington's leading performance is not only weak, I would go as far as calling it inept. A strong, distinctive voice and expressive face are waaaaay beyond this limited actor. Zoe Saldana saves the movie in acting terms.

**MILD SPOILER**

Everyone else is risible including Giovanni Ribisi whose character is possibly set up for the sequel.
